title: Acute asthma exacerbation (adult)
subject: respiratory
summary: Grade severity by speech, respiratory rate, SpO2 and PEF; give inhaled salbutamol (with ipratropium if moderate or severe), oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92% (target 92 to 95%), prednisolone 40 to 50 mg within 1 hour, IV magnesium for poor responders, and discharge on ICS-containing treatment with review in 2 to 7 days.

sections.title: Grade severity (GINA 2026, SIGN 158)
items: Mild: talks in sentences, can lie down, no or mild accessory muscle use, SpO2 on air 94% or more, PEF or FEV1 above 70% of best or predicted.
Moderate: talks in phrases, prefers sitting, accessory muscle use, reduced air entry, SpO2 on air 92% or more, PEF or FEV1 50 to 70%.

Severe (any one): unable to speak, drink or lie down; SpO2 on air below 92%; respiratory rate above 30/min; quiet chest; PEF or FEV1 below 50%. SIGN 158 also uses heart rate 110/min or more and respiratory rate 25/min or more.

Life-threatening: drowsiness, confusion, cyanosis, exhaustion, poor respiratory effort, silent chest, hypotension or arrhythmia, PEF below 33%, PaO2 below 8 kPa (60 mmHg) or a 'normal' PaCO2 of 4.6 to 6.0 kPa. A raised PaCO2 means near-fatal asthma.

Red flags for fatal asthma: previous intubation, hospitalisation or repeated emergency visits in the past year, current or recent oral steroids, no ICS or poor adherence, more than one salbutamol canister a month, psychiatric or psychosocial problems, food allergy or anaphylaxis.

Consider mimics: pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, inducible laryngeal obstruction, pneumonia, acute heart failure, pulmonary embolism. If anaphylaxis features are present, give IM adrenaline first, then bronchodilators.

sections.title: First hour
items: Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92%, titrated to 92 to 95% and no higher than 96% (GINA 2026). SIGN 158 targets 94 to 98%. Never withhold oxygen because an oximeter is unavailable.
Mild: salbutamol 4 puffs (100 mcg/puff) by pMDI and spacer, or budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg 2 inhalations. Review, and repeat once after 30 to 60 minutes only if needed.

Moderate: salbutamol 4 to 6 puffs plus ipratropium 4 puffs (20 mcg/puff) by pMDI and spacer, or nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg plus ipratropium 0.25 mg. Repeat up to 3 times, 20 to 30 minutes apart, if needed.

Severe: salbutamol 6 to 10 puffs plus ipratropium 4 puffs by pMDI and spacer, or nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 0.25 mg, up to 3 times 20 to 30 minutes apart. Life-threatening: oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV access, call ICU or anaesthesia.
Shake the pMDI immediately before every puff and give one puff at a time through the spacer; use tidal breathing if too breathless to breath-hold.

Systemic corticosteroid within 1 hour for all but the mildest attacks: prednisolone 40 to 50 mg orally once daily. If vomiting, unable to swallow or ventilated: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 hours (SIGN 158; GINA uses 200 mg/day in divided doses).

sections.title: Investigations
items: PEF or FEV1 before treatment if it does not delay care (not in life-threatening attacks), at 1 hour, and before discharge.

Arterial blood gas if SpO2 is below 92%, PEF below 50%, any life-threatening feature, or poor response. PaO2 below 60 mmHg (8 kPa) with a normal or raised PaCO2 (especially above 45 mmHg, 6 kPa) indicates respiratory failure.
Chest X-ray is not routine: request it for suspected pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum or consolidation, life-threatening asthma, failure to respond, or need for ventilation.
Serum potassium and glucose in severe attacks (beta2-agonists and steroids cause hypokalaemia); lactate if high-dose or IV salbutamol is being given.

sections.title: Poor response: add-on therapy
items: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes, single dose, for a severe attack not responding to initial bronchodilators (persistent hypoxaemia or PEF below 50%). SIGN 158 gives 1.2 to 2 g with senior review. Nebulised magnesium is not recommended.

Further salbutamol as needed at 15 to 30 minute intervals, or continuous nebulisation 5 to 10 mg/hour for poor responders (SIGN 158). Continue nebulised ipratropium 0.5 mg every 4 to 6 hours in severe or life-threatening asthma.
Watch for SABA toxicity (tachycardia, tremor, hypokalaemia, lactic acidosis): the compensatory hyperventilation can be mistaken for worsening asthma and lead to even more salbutamol.

IV aminophylline is not recommended routinely. SIGN 158 allows it after senior consultation in near-fatal or life-threatening asthma with poor response: 5 mg/kg over 20 minutes (omit the load if already on oral theophylline), then 0.5 to 0.7 mg/kg/hour with daily levels.

Do not give sedatives. Antibiotics only with clear evidence of bacterial infection (fever with purulent sputum, or consolidation). IV beta2-agonists, heliox and leukotriene antagonists are not routine.
Correct hypokalaemia and dehydration. Continue the patient's ICS throughout.

sections.title: Review and admission
items: Reassess symptoms, respiratory rate, SpO2, air entry and PEF after the first bronchodilator dose, at 1 hour, then at least hourly.

Admit if not improving, SpO2 below 92% on room air, SABA needed more often than every 1 to 2 hours, dyspnoea persisting 4 to 6 hours after systemic steroids, or red flags for asthma death (GINA 2026). Admit any life-threatening or near-fatal feature (SIGN 158).

Lower threshold to admit (SIGN 158): previous near-fatal attack, attack despite adequate oral steroid before arrival, presentation at night, living alone, adherence or psychosocial concerns, pregnancy.

sections.title: Escalate to ICU
items: Refer to ICU for deteriorating PEF, persisting or worsening hypoxia, hypercapnia, falling pH, exhaustion or feeble respiration, drowsiness, confusion or respiratory arrest.
Intubation should be done by an experienced operator. Evidence for NIV is weak: if tried, monitor closely, never in agitated patients, and never sedate to allow NIV.
ECMO may be considered for near-fatal asthma refractory to conventional ventilation where available.

sections.title: Discharge
items: Discharge when symptoms meet mild criteria for at least 1 to 2 hours after the last salbutamol, SpO2 92% or more on room air, PEF or FEV1 above 70% of best or predicted, and home support is adequate (GINA 2026).
Prednisolone 40 to 50 mg once daily for a total of 5 to 7 days; no taper is needed if the patient is taking ICS.

Never discharge on SABA alone. Preferred: budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg maintenance and reliever therapy at Step 4 (2 inhalations twice daily plus 1 as needed). If MART is unavailable, medium-dose ICS-LABA or increase the current ICS dose for 2 to 4 weeks.

Check inhaler technique, give a written action plan, review within 2 to 7 days, and refer to a specialist after any ICU admission or if there has been another exacerbation needing OCS or urgent care in the past 12 months.

sections.title: Pregnancy and older adults
items: Pregnancy: treat as for a non-pregnant adult, including nebulised beta2-agonists, early oral steroids and IV magnesium; undertreatment is the main danger (SIGN 158).
Acute severe asthma in pregnancy is an emergency: treat in hospital, keep SpO2 94 to 98%, use continuous fetal monitoring, and involve obstetric and critical care teams early.
Older adults: actively look for an alternative or complicating cardiopulmonary process (heart failure, COPD, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia) and have a lower threshold for chest X-ray (GINA 2026).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: A 'normal' PaCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is a life-threatening sign, not reassurance.
Repeated salbutamol without review; rising respiratory rate from SABA-induced lactic acidosis treated as worsening asthma.
Routine chest X-ray or antibiotics; omitting or delaying systemic steroids.
Discharge without ICS-containing treatment, action plan and early follow-up.

drugs.name: Salbutamol
drugs.dose: pMDI 100 mcg/puff with spacer: 4 puffs (mild), 4 to 6 puffs (moderate), 6 to 10 puffs (severe), up to 3 times 20 to 30 minutes apart in the first hour; or nebulised 2.5 mg (moderate) to 5 mg (severe)
drugs.notes: Continuous nebulisation 5 to 10 mg/hour for poor responders (SIGN 158). Monitor potassium, heart rate and lactate.

drugs.name: Ipratropium bromide
drugs.dose: 4 puffs (20 mcg/puff) by pMDI and spacer, or 0.25 mg nebulised with each salbutamol dose in the first hour; 0.5 mg nebulised every 4 to 6 hours in severe attacks (SIGN 158)
drugs.notes: Moderate, severe or life-threatening attacks; little benefit after the first 1 to 2 hours in most patients.

drugs.name: Budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg
drugs.dose: 2 inhalations for a mild attack; at discharge 2 inhalations twice daily plus 1 as needed (MART Step 4)
drugs.notes: Seek care if more than 12 inhalations are needed in 24 hours.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.dose: 40 to 50 mg orally once daily for 5 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Give within 1 hour of arrival; no taper needed if on ICS.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.notes: Only if oral route not possible (vomiting, too breathless, ventilated). GINA uses 200 mg/day in divided doses.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.dose: 2 g IV over 20 minutes, single dose (SIGN 158: 1.2 to 2 g)
drugs.notes: Severe attack not responding to initial treatment. Repeat doses not assessed; risk of hypermagnesaemia.

drugs.name: Aminophylline
drugs.dose: 5 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes, then 0.5 to 0.7 mg/kg/hour
drugs.notes: Not routine. Senior decision only; omit loading dose if on oral theophylline; check levels daily.

sources.title: Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2026 update (Box 9-6, acute care facility flowchart)
SIGN 158: British guideline on the management of asthma (acute asthma sections, 2024 revision, May 2025 corrections)
